Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿except one who maneuvers for combat﴾, that he said: "That means one who feigns retreat, intending to return to attack the polytheists." ﴿or withdraws to a group﴾, that is, or withdraws to his companions without having been defeated. ﴿then he has earned wrath from God﴾, that is, they deserved anger from God. ﴿And his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾. He said: "This was specifically on the Day of Badr, and it was severe for the Muslims on that day, so that He might cut off the remnant of the unbelievers. It was the first battle in which the Muslims fought the polytheists of Mecca."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "The *mutaharrif* is one who advances ahead of his companions, who sees a weakness in the enemy and strikes it. The *mutahayyiz* is one who flees to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and likewise whoever flees today to his commander and his companions."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah concerning His saying: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾, that he said: "This verse is abrogated by the verse in al-Anfal: ﴿Now God has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ (al-Anfal: 66), the verse."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* (and the wording is his), Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan*, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "We were on a military campaign, and the people panicked and fled in confusion. We said: How can we meet the Messenger of God ﷺ when we have fled from the advance and returned with wrath? So we came to the Messenger of God before the dawn prayer. He came out and said: 'Who are the people?' We said: 'We are the fleeing ones.' He said: 'No, rather you are the returning ones (*al-'akkarun*).' We kissed his hand, and he said: 'I am your *fi'ah*, and I am the *fi'ah* of the Muslims.' Then he recited: ﴿except one who maneuvers for combat or withdraws to a group﴾."

Hadiths have been reported prohibiting fleeing from the advance and stating that it is among the major sins, and a group of the Companions reported that it is among the major sins, as Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿So you did not kill them﴾, that he said: "This was said to the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ when they said: 'I killed this one, and I killed that one.'" ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ was said to Muhammad ﷺ when he threw pebbles at the unbelievers.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾, that he said: "He threw at them with pebbles on the Day of Badr."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verse 15–18 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hakim ibn Hizam, who said: "When the Day of Badr came, we heard a sound from the sky to the earth (p-532), as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw that gravel and said: 'May the faces be disfigured!' and we were routed. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾, the verse."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, who said: "I heard the sound of pebbles falling from the sky on the Day of Badr, as if they had fallen into a basin. When the people lined up, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took them and threw them into the faces of the polytheists, and they fled. This is His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw.﴾"

al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated "from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah said to Ali: 'Hand me a handful of gravel.' So he handed it to him, and he threw it into the faces of the people, and not one of the people remained except that his eyes were filled with the gravel. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw.﴾"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "When the Day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf began to spur his horse until he came near the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and some men of the Muslims intercepted Ubayy ibn Khalaf to kill him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'Hold back!' So they held back. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took his spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it broke one of his ribs. Ubayy ibn Khalaf returned to his companions, heavy (wounded), and they carried him when they turned back, returning. They began saying: 'There is no harm.' Ubayy said when they said that to him: 'By Allah, if it had been among the people, it would have killed them. Did he not say: I will kill you, if Allah wills?' His companions took him along, supporting him, until he died in part of the way, and they buried him." Ibn al-Musayyib said: "Concerning that, Allah revealed: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw.﴾"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhri something similar to it, and its chain of transmission to both of them is sound. Al-Hakim also narrated it in al-Mustadrak.

Ibn Kathir said: This statement from these two imams is very strange, and perhaps they meant that the verse encompasses them through its generality. Likewise said Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr, as will come.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr: "That on the Day of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for a bow and shot with it at the fortress, and the arrow came until it killed Ibn Abi al-Huqayq in his bed. So Allah revealed: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw.﴾"

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying: ﴿But Allah threw﴾, i.e., that throw was not by your throwing, were it not for what Allah made of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy, until He routed them. ﴿And that He might test the believers with a fine trial from Him﴾, i.e., that the believers might recognize from His blessing upon them in granting them victory over their enemy despite the abundance of their enemy and the fewness of their number, so that by that they might know His right and give thanks for His blessing.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verses 15–18 (part 1 of 2)**

*Al-zahf* (the advance of troops) means drawing near gradually, little by little. Its original sense is pushing forward on the buttocks, and then every person walking toward another in battle was called *zahif* (advancing). *Al-tazahuf* means approaching and drawing close. You say: *zahafa ila al-'aduww zahfan* (he advanced toward the enemy in an advance), and *izdahafa al-qawm* (the people advanced), meaning some of them walked toward others. The accusative *zahfan* may be either a verbal noun for a verb that is omitted, meaning *tazhafuna zahfan* (you advance in an advance), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to the believers, meaning while you are advancing toward the unbelievers; or a circumstantial clause referring to those who disbelieved, meaning while the unbelievers are advancing toward you; or a circumstantial clause referring to both parties, meaning mutually advancing. ﴿So do not turn your backs to them﴾. God forbade the believers to flee from the unbelievers when they meet them, and when some of them have moved toward others for combat. The apparent meaning of this verse is general, covering all believers at all times and in all circumstances, except the case of *taharruf* (maneuvering) and *tahayyuz* (withdrawing to a group).

It has been reported from 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Sa'id, Abu Nadrah, 'Ikrimah, Nafi', al-Hasan, Qatadah, Zayd ibn Abi Habib, and al-Dahhak that the prohibition on fleeing from the advance in this verse is specific to the Day of Badr, and that the people of Badr were not permitted to withdraw. Had they withdrawn, they would have withdrawn to the polytheists, since on that day there were no Muslims on earth other than themselves, and they had no *fi'ah* (group) except the Prophet ﷺ. After that, however, some of them became a *fi'ah* for others. This is also the view of Abu Hanifah.

They said: This is supported by His saying: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾, for it refers to the Day of Badr. It has also been said that this verse is abrogated (*mansukhah*) by the verse of weakness (*ayat al-di'f*).

Most scholars held that this verse is *muhkamah* (firm and not abrogated), general and not specific, and that fleeing from the advance is forbidden. This is supported by the fact that this verse was revealed after the battle of Badr had ended.

As for the first group's view, it is answered that the reference in *yawma'idhin* (on that day) to the Day of Badr is not correct, since the reference is to the day of the advance, as the context indicates. There is no contradiction between this verse and the verse of weakness; rather, this verse is qualified by it, so fleeing from the advance is forbidden under the condition that God specified in the verse of weakness. There is no basis for what they said, that there were no Muslims on earth on the Day of Badr other than those who were present there, for in Medina at that time there was a large number of people whom the Prophet ﷺ did not order to go out, because he and those who went out with him did not initially think that there would be fighting.

This is supported by the authentic reports that explicitly state that fleeing from the advance is among the major sins (*al-kaba'ir*), as in the hadith: "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and within it: "and turning away on the day of the advance," and similar hadiths. This topic has long ramifications and many branches, and it is explained in its proper places.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *al-adbar* is the plural of *dubur* (back), and the expression "back" in this verse is eloquent, because of the disgrace it implies for the fleeing man and the blame directed at him.

His saying: ﴿except one who maneuvers for combat﴾. *Al-taharruf* is departing from the straight direction. What is meant here is moving from one side to another in the battlefield, seeking the stratagems of war and deceiving the enemy. It includes feigning defeat so that the enemy pursues, then turning back on them and gaining control over them, and similar war tactics, for war is deception.

His saying: ﴿or one who withdraws to a group﴾, that is, to a group of Muslims other than the group facing the enemy. The accusative of *muta-harrifan* and *mutahayyizan* is by exception from those who turn away, meaning: whoever turns his back to them, except a man of theirs who maneuvers or withdraws. They may also be in the accusative as circumstantial clauses, and the particle of exception would then be *laghw* (superfluous) with no governing function. The clause ﴿he has earned wrath from God﴾ is the answer to the condition.

The meaning is: whoever flees and retreats from the advance has returned with wrath from God, except one who maneuvers or withdraws. ﴿And his refuge is Hell﴾, that is, the place to which he retreats is the Fire. Thus his flight leads him to something more severe in affliction than what he fled from, and greater in punishment.

*Al-ma'wa* is the place to which a person retreats. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾ means what he arrives at is the torment of the Fire.

This verse includes this severe threat for whoever flees from the advance, and in this is evidence that it is among the destructive major sins.

His saying: ﴿So you did not kill them, but God killed them﴾. The *fa'* (so) is the answer to an implied condition, meaning: if you know what God has related to you of His aid to you with angels and His casting terror into their hearts, then you did not kill them, but God killed them through the means He facilitated for you that necessitate victory.

His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾.

The commentators differed about this throwing in several views. It has been reported from Malik that what is meant is what the Prophet ﷺ did on the Day of Hunayn, when he threw a handful of pebbles from the valley at the polytheists, and it struck each one of them. It has also been said that what is meant is the throw by which the Messenger of God ﷺ struck Ubayy ibn Khalaf in the neck with a spear, and he fled and died from it. It has also been said that what is meant is the arrow that the Messenger of God ﷺ shot at the fortress of Khaybar, and it traveled through the air until it struck Ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. These views are weak, for the verse was revealed right after the battle of Badr.

Also, the well-known account in the books of biography (*siyar*) and hadith about the killing of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq is that it occurred in a different form from this.

The correct view, as Ibn Ishaq and others said, is that the throwing mentioned in this verse is what the Prophet ﷺ did on the Day of Badr, for he took a handful of dust and threw it into the faces of the polytheists, and it struck each one of them and entered their eyes, nostrils and noses.

Tha'lab said: The meaning of ﴿And you did not throw﴾ is the fear and terror in their hearts when you threw the pebbles, and they fled. ﴿But God threw﴾, that is, He helped you and granted you victory. The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning He helped you, granted you victory, and arranged matters for you.

Abu 'Ubaydah also related something similar in *Kitab al-Majaz*.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: The meaning of ﴿And you did not throw﴾ is by your own strength, ﴿when you threw﴾, but rather by the strength of God you threw. It has also been said: The meaning is that this throw with the handful of dust which you threw was not really thrown by you, for if you had thrown it, its effect would not have reached beyond what human throwing reaches. Rather, it was God's throw, since it produced that great effect. Thus He affirmed the throwing to the Messenger of God ﷺ because its form was produced by him, and He negated it from him because its effect, which no human can bear, is the act of God, Mighty and Majestic. So God is the true agent of the throw, as though it had never existed from the Messenger of God ﷺ at all. Thus it is in *al-Kashshaf*.

His saying: ﴿and that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him﴾. *Al-bala'* here means favor, and the meaning is: that He might bestow a beautiful favor upon the believers. The *lam* is connected to an omitted element, meaning: and for the sake of bestowing His beautiful favors upon them He did this and not for anything else. Or the *waw* is conjunctive, linking what follows to an implied cause before it, meaning: but God threw so that He might destroy the unbelievers and that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him. ﴿Indeed God is Hearing and Knowing﴾, Hearing their supplication and Knowing their circumstances.

The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to the good trial, and it is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the purpose is ﴿that﴾. ﴿And that God is the one who weakens the plot of the unbelievers﴾, meaning: its purpose from Him, glorified is He, by what occurred of what the preceding verses related, is to test the believers and to weaken the plot of the unbelievers. It has also been said that what is referred to is the killing and the throwing.

It has been read with the *ha'* (in *muhinu*) doubled and with it single with tanwin. Al-Hasan read it with the *ha'* single and in construct form (idafah).

*Al-kayd* is scheming, and its explanation has already preceded.

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Nafi' that he asked Ibn 'Umar, saying: "We are a people who do not stand firm when fighting our enemy, and we do not know who the *fi'ah* is in front of us, or our army?" He said to me: "The *fi'ah* is the Messenger of God ﷺ." I said: "God says: ﴿When you meet those who disbelieve advancing, do not turn your backs to them﴾." There is no contradiction between this verse and the verse of weakness; rather, this verse is qualified by it, so fleeing from the advance is forbidden under the condition that God specified in the verse of weakness. There is no basis for what they said, that there were no Muslims on earth on the Day of Badr other than those who were present there, for in Medina at that time there was a large number of people whom the Prophet ﷺ did not order to go out, because he and those who went out with him did not initially think that there would be fighting.

This is supported by the authentic reports that explicitly state that fleeing from the advance is among the major sins (*al-kaba'ir*), as in the hadith: "Avoid the seven destructive sins," and within it: "and turning away on the day of the advance," and similar hadiths. This topic has long ramifications and many branches, and it is explained in its proper places.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *al-adbar* is the plural of *dubur* (back), and the expression "back" in this verse is eloquent, because of the disgrace it implies for the fleeing man and the blame directed at him.

His saying: ﴿except one who maneuvers for combat﴾. *Al-taharruf* is departing from the straight direction. What is meant here is moving from one side to another in the battlefield, seeking the stratagems of war and deceiving the enemy. It includes feigning defeat so that the enemy pursues, then turning back on them and gaining control over them, and similar war tactics, for war is deception.

His saying: ﴿or one who withdraws to a group﴾, that is, to a group of Muslims other than the group facing the enemy. The accusative of *muta-harrifan* and *mutahayyizan* is by exception from those who turn away, meaning: whoever turns his back to them, except a man of theirs who maneuvers or withdraws. They may also be in the accusative as circumstantial clauses, and the particle of exception would then be *laghw* (superfluous) with no governing function. The clause ﴿he has earned wrath from God﴾ is the answer to the condition.

The meaning is: whoever flees and retreats from the advance has returned with wrath from God, except one who maneuvers or withdraws. ﴿And his refuge is Hell﴾, that is, the place to which he retreats is the Fire. Thus his flight leads him to something more severe in affliction than what he fled from, and greater in punishment.

*Al-ma'wa* is the place to which a person retreats. ﴿And wretched is the destination﴾ means what he arrives at is the torment of the Fire.

This verse includes this severe threat for whoever flees from the advance, and in this is evidence that it is among the destructive major sins.

His saying: ﴿So you did not kill them, but God killed them﴾. The *fa'* (so) is the answer to an implied condition, meaning: if you know what God has related to you of His aid to you with angels and His casting terror into their hearts, then you did not kill them, but God killed them through the means He facilitated for you that necessitate victory.

His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but God threw﴾.

The commentators differed about this throwing in several views. It has been reported from Malik that what is meant is what the Prophet ﷺ did on the Day of Hunayn, when he threw a handful of pebbles from the valley at the polytheists, and it struck each one of them. It has also been said that what is meant is the throw by which the Messenger of God ﷺ struck Ubayy ibn Khalaf in the neck with a spear, and he fled and died from it. It has also been said that what is meant is the arrow that the Messenger of God ﷺ shot at the fortress of Khaybar, and it traveled through the air until it struck Ibn Abi al-Huqayq while he was on his bed. These views are weak, for the verse was revealed right after the battle of Badr.

Also, the well-known account in the books of biography (*siyar*) and hadith about the killing of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq is that it occurred in a different form from this.

The correct view, as Ibn Ishaq and others said, is that the throwing mentioned in this verse is what the Prophet ﷺ did on the Day of Badr, for he took a handful of dust and threw it into the faces of the polytheists, and it struck each one of them and entered their eyes, nostrils and noses.

Tha'lab said: The meaning of ﴿And you did not throw﴾ is the fear and terror in their hearts when you threw the pebbles, and they fled. ﴿But God threw﴾, that is, He helped you and granted you victory. The Arabs say: "God threw for you," meaning He helped you, granted you victory, and arranged matters for you.

Abu 'Ubaydah also related something similar in *Kitab al-Majaz*.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: The meaning of ﴿And you did not throw﴾ is by your own strength, ﴿when you threw﴾, but rather by the strength of God you threw. It has also been said: The meaning is that this throw with the handful of dust which you threw was not really thrown by you, for if you had thrown it, its effect would not have reached beyond what human throwing reaches. Rather, it was God's throw, since it produced that great effect. Thus He affirmed the throwing to the Messenger of God ﷺ because its form was produced by him, and He negated it from him because its effect, which no human can bear, is the act of God, Mighty and Majestic. So God is the true agent of the throw, as though it had never existed from the Messenger of God ﷺ at all. Thus it is in *al-Kashshaf*.

His saying: ﴿and that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him﴾. *Al-bala'* here means favor, and the meaning is: that He might bestow a beautiful favor upon the believers. The *lam* is connected to an omitted element, meaning: and for the sake of bestowing His beautiful favors upon them He did this and not for anything else. Or the *waw* is conjunctive, linking what follows to an implied cause before it, meaning: but God threw so that He might destroy the unbelievers and that He might test the believers with a good trial from Him. ﴿Indeed God is Hearing and Knowing﴾, Hearing their supplication and Knowing their circumstances.

The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to the good trial, and it is in the nominative case as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: the purpose is ﴿that﴾. ﴿And that God is the one who weakens the plot of the unbelievers﴾, meaning: its purpose from Him, glorified is He, by what occurred of what the preceding verses related, is to test the believers and to weaken the plot of the unbelievers. It has also been said that what is referred to is the killing and the throwing.

It has been read with the *ha'* (in *muhinu*) doubled and with it single with tanwin. Al-Hasan read it with the *ha'* single and in construct form (idafah).

*Al-kayd* is scheming, and its explanation has already preceded.

Al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Nafi' that he asked Ibn 'Umar, saying: "We are a people who do not stand firm when fighting our enemy, and we do not know who the *fi'ah* is in front of us, or our army?" He said to me: "The *fi'ah* is the Messenger of God ﷺ." I said: "God says: ﴿When you meet those who disbelieve advancing, do not turn your backs to them﴾." He said: "This verse was only revealed about the people of Badr, not before it nor after it."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh*, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri concerning His saying: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾, the verse, that he said: "It was only for the people of Badr specifically."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab who said: "Do not let this verse deceive you, for it was only on the Day of Badr, and I am a *fi'ah* for every Muslim."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, that he said: "It was revealed specifically about the people of Badr, that it was not permitted for them to flee from the Messenger of God ﷺ and abandon him."

It has been reported that the restriction of this verse to the people of Badr is from a group of the Successors (*tabi'un*) and those after them, and we have already mentioned this.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His saying: ﴿except one who maneuvers for combat﴾, that he said: "That means one who feigns retreat, intending to return to attack the polytheists." ﴿or withdraws to a group﴾, that is, or withdraws to his companions without having been defeated. ﴿then he has earned wrath from God﴾, that is, they deserved anger from God. ﴿And his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾. He said: "This was specifically on the Day of Badr, and it was severe for the Muslims on that day, so that He might cut off the remnant of the unbelievers. It was the first battle in which the Muslims fought the polytheists of Mecca."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Dahhak, who said: "The *mutaharrif* is one who advances ahead of his companions, who sees a weakness in the enemy and strikes it. The *mutahayyiz* is one who flees to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and likewise whoever flees today to his commander and his companions."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah concerning His saying: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾, that he said: "This verse is abrogated by the verse in al-Anfal: ﴿Now God has lightened [the burden] for you﴾ (al-Anfal: 66), the verse."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* (and the wording is his), Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan*, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Nahhas, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "We were on a military campaign, and the people panicked and fled in confusion. We said: How can we meet the Messenger of God ﷺ when we have fled from the advance and returned with wrath? So we came to the Messenger of God before the dawn prayer. He came out and said: 'Who are the people?' We said: 'We are the fleeing ones.' He said: 'No, rather you are the returning ones (*al-'akkarun*).' We kissed his hand, and he said: 'I am your *fi'ah*, and I am the *fi'ah* of the Muslims.' Then he recited: ﴿except one who maneuvers for combat or withdraws to a group﴾."

Hadiths have been reported prohibiting fleeing from the advance and stating that it is among the major sins, and a group of the Companions reported that it is among the major sins, as Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Ibn 'Umar.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿So you did not kill them﴾, that he said: "This was said to the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ when they said: 'I killed this one, and I killed that one.'" ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ was said to Muhammad ﷺ when he threw pebbles at the unbelievers.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾, that he said: "He threw at them with pebbles on the Day of Badr."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verse 15–18 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Hakim ibn Hizam, who said: "When the Day of Badr came, we heard a sound from the sky to the earth (p-532), as if it were the sound of a pebble falling into a basin. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw that gravel and said: 'May the faces be disfigured!' and we were routed. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾, the verse."

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir, who said: "I heard the sound of pebbles falling from the sky on the Day of Badr, as if they had fallen into a basin. When the people lined up, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took them and threw them into the faces of the polytheists, and they fled. This is His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw.﴾"

al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated "from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾, he said: The Messenger of Allah said to Ali: 'Hand me a handful of gravel.' So he handed it to him, and he threw it into the faces of the people, and not one of the people remained except that his eyes were filled with the gravel. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw.﴾"

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "When the Day of Uhud came, Ubayy ibn Khalaf began to spur his horse until he came near the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and some men of the Muslims intercepted Ubayy ibn Khalaf to kill him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: 'Hold back!' So they held back. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took his spear in his hand and threw it at Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it broke one of his ribs. Ubayy ibn Khalaf returned to his companions, heavy (wounded), and they carried him when they turned back, returning. They began saying: 'There is no harm.' Ubayy said when they said that to him: 'By Allah, if it had been among the people, it would have killed them. Did he not say: I will kill you, if Allah wills?' His companions took him along, supporting him, until he died in part of the way, and they buried him." Ibn al-Musayyib said: "Concerning that, Allah revealed: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw.﴾"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Zuhri something similar to it, and its chain of transmission to both of them is sound. Al-Hakim also narrated it in al-Mustadrak.

Ibn Kathir said: This statement from these two imams is very strange, and perhaps they meant that the verse encompasses them through its generality. Likewise said Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr, as will come.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr: "That on the Day of Ibn Abi al-Huqayq, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called for a bow and shot with it at the fortress, and the arrow came until it killed Ibn Abi al-Huqayq in his bed. So Allah revealed: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw.﴾"

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying: ﴿But Allah threw﴾, i.e., that throw was not by your throwing, were it not for what Allah made of your victory and what He cast into the hearts of your enemy, until He routed them. ﴿And that He might test the believers with a fine trial from Him﴾, i.e., that the believers might recognize from His blessing upon them in granting them victory over their enemy despite the abundance of their enemy and the fewness of their number, so that by that they might know His right and give thanks for His blessing.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verse 19:

Al-istifta'h (الاستفتاح) means seeking victory. Scholars have differed over who is addressed in the verse. It was said that it is addressed to the disbelievers, mockingly. The meaning is: "If you seek victory from Allah over Muhammad, then victory has come to you." When they set out from Makkah, they had asked Allah to grant victory to the more deserving of the two groups, so Allah mocked them and called the destruction that befell them "victory." The rest of the verse, on this view, means: "And if you desist from what you were upon of disbelief and enmity toward the Messenger of Allah, then that [desisting] is better for you. And if you return to what you were upon of disbelief and enmity, We will return by empowering the believers over you and granting them victory, as We empowered them and gave them victory on the Day of Badr." "And your company will not avail you anything, however numerous it may be": that is, your group will not benefit you in any way, even if it is large. In no circumstance will it avail you, not even when it is at its greatest number. Then He said: "And indeed Allah is with the believers," and whoever Allah is with is the one who is victorious, and whoever Allah is against is the one who is forsaken.

It was recited with a kasra and with a fatha on إنّ. With the kasra (إنَّ), it is a resumed sentence (al-istin'af, a new independent clause). With the fatha (أنَّ), it is read as an elliptical construction, meaning: "And because Allah is with the believers, He did that."

It was also said that the verse is addressed to the believers. The meaning is: "If you seek victory from Allah, then victory has come to you on the Day of Badr. And if you desist from the like of what you did, namely taking spoils and ransoming prisoners before permission was given to you to do so, then that is better for you. And if you return to the like of that, We will return to rebuking you, as in His words: ﴿Had there not been a decree from Allah that preceded﴾ [8:68]," and so on. It is not hidden that this view is contradicted by the meaning of "your company will not avail you anything," and is also contradicted by "And indeed Allah is with the believers." Interpreting it this way is possible only with forced and strained effort.

It was also said that the address in ﴿If you seek a decision, then the decision has come to you﴾ is to the believers, while what follows it is to the disbelievers. But there is no hiding the disruption this causes to the structure of the text, and the return of pronouns that run in one pattern in the speech back to two different groups.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Ibn Mandah, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (Dala'il al-Nubuwwah) reported from Ibn Shihab, from Abd Allah ibn Tha'labah ibn Sughayr, that Abu Jahl said when the two groups met: "O Allah, sever us from kinship and bring to us what we do not know, so destroy him tomorrow morning." That was his seeking of victory, so the verse was revealed: ﴿If you seek victory﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Atiyyah, who said: Abu Jahl said on the Day of Badr: "O Allah, grant victory to the more guided of the two groups, the better of the two groups, and the best of the two groups," so the verse was revealed.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿If you seek victory﴾: it means the polytheists, that is, "If you seek help, then reinforcement has come to you."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from Mujahid, regarding ﴿If you seek victory, then victory has come to you﴾: the disbelieving Quraysh said, "Our Lord, decide between us and Muhammad and his companions," so He decided between them on the Day of Badr.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿If you seek victory﴾: "If you seek judgment, then judgment has come to you on the Day of Badr."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi, regarding His words ﴿And if you desist﴾: "From fighting Muhammad (ﷺ)." ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾: "If you seek victory a second time, I will grant victory to Muhammad." ﴿And indeed Allah is with the believers﴾: "With Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions."

Abd ibn Humayd reported from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾: he said, "We will return to you with capture and killing."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verses 20–23:

Allah – glorified is He – commanded the believers to obey Him and to obey His Messenger, and forbade them from turning away from His Messenger. So the pronoun in "ʿanhu" (from him) refers to the Messenger, because obedience to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is part of obedience to Allah, and ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ (al-Nisa’: 80). It is also possible that this pronoun refers to Allah and to His Messenger, as in His saying: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ (al-Tawbah: 62). It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the matter indicated by "aṭīʿū" (obey). The original form of "tawallaw" is "tatawallaw", and one of the two tā’s was dropped. This is the explanation of the verse according to the apparent address to the believers, and it is the view of the majority (al-jumhur). It has also been said that it is an address to the hypocrites, and the meaning is: O you who have believed with their tongues only.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "This, although it is possible in a distant sense, is very weak, because Allah described those addressed in this verse as believers, and belief is affirmation (taṣdīq), while the hypocrites do not possess any affirmation at all. Even more remote is the view of the one who said that the address is to the Children of Israel, for it is foreign to the verse." The clause "and you hear" (wa-antum tasmaʿūn) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The meaning: "and you hear what is recited to you of proofs and evidences and you affirm them, and you are not like the deaf and the mute."

﴿And do not be like those who say, "We hear"﴾, and they are the polytheists, or the hypocrites, or the Jews, or all of these together, for they hear with their ears without understanding or acting, so they are like one who has not heard at all, because he has not benefited from what he heard.

Then Allah – glorified is He – informed that the worst of creatures (al-dawābb, i.e., whatever crawls upon the earth) "in the sight of Allah" – that is, in His judgment – are "the deaf, the mute", that is, those who neither hear nor speak. They are described thus although they are among those who hear and speak, because they do not benefit from hearing and speaking. ﴿Who do not reason﴾, that is, they do not understand what is beneficial to them so that they may pursue it, and what is harmful to them so that they may avoid it. Therefore they are the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah, because even other animals discern to some degree and distinguish between what benefits them and what harms them.

﴿And if Allah had known any good in them﴾, that is, in these deaf and mute ones, ﴿He would have made them hear﴾, a hearing by which they would benefit, and by which they would understand the proofs and evidences.

Al-Zajjaj said: "He would have made them hear" means the answer to everything they asked about. It has also been said: He would have made them hear the speech of the dead whom they asked to be revived, for they asked for the revival of Qusayy ibn Kilab and others, so that they might testify to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse﴾, because it had already preceded in His knowledge that they would not believe. The clause "while they were averse" (wa-hum muʿriḍūn) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh have related from Mujahid, regarding His saying ﴿and they do not hear﴾, that he said: "Angry."

Ibn Abi Hatim has related from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: "This verse was revealed concerning so-and-so and his companions."

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in the sight of Allah﴾, that he said: "They are a group of Quraysh from the Banu ʿAbd al-Dar."

Ibn Abi Hatim has related from him regarding His saying ﴿the deaf, the mute, who do not reason﴾, that he said: "They do not follow the truth."

Ibn al-Mundhir has related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his people, and perhaps he is the one referred to by 'so-and-so' in the earlier statement of ʿAli – may Allah be pleased with him."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾, that is, He would have made their words, which they uttered with their tongues, effective for them; but their hearts opposed that in them.

Abu al-Shaykh has related from ʿIkrimah regarding the verse, that he said: "They said: 'We are deaf to what Muhammad calls us to; we do not hear it. We are mute; we do not answer him with affirmation in it.' They were all killed at Uhud, and they were the standard-bearers on the day of Uhud."

The command here to respond reinforces the earlier command to obey. He used the singular pronoun in "when He calls you," as He did in His words, "and do not turn away" (al-Anfal: 20). We have already discussed the reason for this.

The word *istijaba* (to respond) means obedience.

Abu 'Ubayda said: The meaning of *istajibu* (respond) is *ajibu* (answer). Although *istajaba* takes the preposition *li-* (to), *ajaba* can take the object directly, as in His words: ﴿O our people, answer the caller of Allah﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 31). *Istajaba* can also take the object directly, as in the words of the poet:

As for His words, ﴿when He calls you to that which gives you life﴾, the *lam* (to) is connected to *istajibu* (respond). The meaning is: respond to that which gives you life when He calls you. There is no obstacle to its being connected to *da'akum* (calls you), meaning: when He calls you to that in which your life lies, namely the sciences of the Shari'ah (Islamic law). Knowledge is life, just as ignorance is death, so "life" here is used metaphorically for knowledge.

The majority of exegetes (*al-Jumhur min al-mufassirin*) said: The meaning is, respond to obedience and to what the Qur'an contains of commands and prohibitions, for in it is everlasting life and perpetual blessing. It was also said that what is meant by His words, "that which gives you life," is jihad, for it is the apparent cause of life, since if the enemy is not fought, it will attack. This command to respond is used as evidence that every Muslim, when the word of Allah or the word of His Messenger reaches him concerning a legal ruling of the Shari'ah, must hasten to act upon it, whatever it may be, and abandon whatever contradicts it of personal opinion or the sayings of men.

In this noble verse is the greatest incentive to act upon the texts of the evidences, to abandon strict adherence to the schools of thought (*al-madhahib*), and to disregard whatever contradicts what is in the Book and the Sunnah, whatever it may be.

His words: ﴿And know that Allah comes between a person and his heart﴾. It was said: its meaning is, hasten to respond before you lose the ability to do so, through the loss of the hearts with which you understand, by the death that Allah has decreed for you. It was also said: its meaning is that the Muslims feared, on the day of Badr, the large number of the enemy, so Allah informed them that He comes between a person and his heart, by changing their fear into security and changing the security of their enemy into fear. It was also said: this is a figurative expression (*tamthil*) for His nearness to the servant, like His words: ﴿And We are nearer to him than his jugular vein﴾ (Qaf: 16). Its meaning is that He knows the inner thoughts of the hearts, and nothing in them is hidden from Him.

Ibn Jarir chose that this is an informative statement from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that He has more power over the hearts of His servants than they do, and that He comes between them and their hearts whenever He wills, so that a person perceives nothing except by His will, the Mighty and Majestic. It is not hidden from you that there is no obstacle to interpreting the verse according to all these meanings. The words ﴿and that to Him you will be gathered﴾ are joined to ﴿that Allah comes between a person and his heart﴾, and that you will be gathered to Him, and He will recompense you, good for good and evil for evil.

Al-Farra' said: If you began a new sentence and gave *inna* (indeed) in "innahu" a kasra (i.e., *innahu* with a kasra on the hamza), it would be correct. Perhaps what he meant is that such a construction is permissible in Arabic.

His words: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have wronged﴾. That is, beware of a trial that extends beyond the wrongdoer, striking both the righteous and the wicked, and its striking is not restricted to those among you who directly commit the wrong.

The grammarians differed concerning the entry of the emphatic *nun* into *tusibanna* (will strike). Al-Farra' said: It is in the same position as your saying: "Dismount from the animal, lest it throw you down" (*la tatrahanka*). It is the response to the imperative, expressed in the form of a prohibition. That is: if you dismount from it, it will not throw you down. A similar example is His words, exalted is He: ﴿Enter your dwellings, lest Solomon and his armies crush you﴾ (al-Naml: 18), meaning: if you enter, they will not crush you. The *nun* entered because the sentence carries the meaning of a condition.

Al-Mubarrad said: It is a prohibition after a command.

The meaning is a prohibition addressed to the wrongdoers: that is, let them not approach wrongdoing. A similar example is what is related from Sibawayh: "Let me not see you here" (*la ara'annaka hahuna*), for its meaning is: "Do not be here," since whoever is here, you will see him.

Al-Jurjani said: "la tusibanna" is a prohibition in the position of an attribute for *fitnatan* (a trial). 'Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy, and Ibn Mas'ud read *latusibanna* (with the *lam* of oath), so that the *lam* is the answer to an omitted oath, and the implied meaning is: "Beware of a trial; by Allah, it will strike those among you who have wronged, exclusively." The meaning of this reading differs from the reading of the majority, since it indicates that the trial strikes only the wrongdoer, unlike the reading of the majority.

His words: ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾. Among the severity of His punishment is that He strikes with punishment those who did not directly engage in its causes. The Qur'anic verses have come that no one is struck except for his own sin, and no one is punished except for his own crime. It is possible to interpret what is in this verse as referring to punishments that come through Allah's giving some servants power over others. It is also possible that this verse is specifically about general punishments, and Allah knows best. It may also be said that those who did not wrong have made themselves liable to punishment through causes such as abandoning the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil, so the affliction that extends from the wrongdoer to others is specific to those who abandon what is obligatory upon them when wrongdoing appears.

His words: ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾. Among the severity of His punishment is that He strikes with punishment those who did not directly engage in its causes. The Qur'anic verses have come that no one is struck except for his own sin, and no one is punished except for his own crime. It is possible to interpret what is in this verse as referring to punishments that come through Allah's giving some servants power over others. It is also possible that this verse is specifically about general punishments, and Allah knows best. It may also be said that those who did not wrong have made themselves liable to punishment through causes such as abandoning the enjoining of good and forbidding of evil, so the affliction that extends from the wrongdoer to others is specific to those who abandon what is obligatory upon them when wrongdoing appears.

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿when He calls you to that which gives you life﴾, that he said: "to the truth."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah concerning the verse, that he said: "It is this Qur'an. In it is life, trust, salvation, and protection in this world and the Hereafter."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr concerning His words: ﴿when He calls you to that which gives you life﴾, that it means: to the war through which Allah honored you after humiliation, strengthened you after weakness, and protected you through it from punishment after they had dominated you.

It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, who said: "I was praying in the mosque, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called me, but I did not answer him. Then I came to him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I was praying.' He said: 'Did not Allah say: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you﴾?'" The hadith continues. In it is evidence for what we mentioned, that the verse includes every call from Allah or from His Messenger.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And know that Allah comes between a person and his heart﴾, that he said: "He comes between the believer and disbelief and the disobedience of Allah, and He comes between the disbeliever and faith and the obedience of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas concerning the verse that he said: "His knowledge comes between a person and his heart."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "He comes between a person and his heart until He leaves him without understanding."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Hasan concerning the verse that he said: "In nearness to Him."

Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Mutarrif, who said: I said to al-Zubayr, "O Abu 'Abd Allah, you neglected the caliph until he was killed, then you came seeking retribution for his blood!" Al-Zubayr said: "We recited during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Uthman: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have wronged﴾, and we did not think that we would be its people, until it fell upon us where it fell."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Hasan who said: "al-Zubayr recited: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike only those among you who have wronged﴾," and said: "It is the calamity and the matter which is to occur."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Hasan concerning the verse that he said: "It was revealed concerning 'Ali, 'Uthman, Talhah, and al-Zubayr."

'Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Dahhak who said: "It was revealed specifically concerning the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi who said: "It was revealed specifically concerning the people of Badr. Then it struck them on the day of the Camel, and they fought one another, and among those killed were Talhah and al-Zubayr, and both of them were from the people of Badr."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi concerning the verse that he said: "It strikes the wrongdoer and the righteous in general."

Abu al-Shaykh related the same from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid concerning the verse that he said: "It is like ﴿He comes between a person and his heart﴾, until He leaves him without understanding."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse that he said: "Allah commanded the believers not to allow wrongdoing to remain among them, lest Allah encompass them all with punishment." And the sound and numerous hadiths have come that when this Ummah does not enjoin good and forbid evil, Allah will encompass them with a punishment from Himself.

(p-٥٣٥)

The address in His words ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ is to the Muhajirun (the Emigrants). That is, remember the time of your fewness. The word ﴿oppressed﴾ (مُسْتَضْعَفُونَ) is a second predicate of the subject. "The earth" means the land of Makkah. "Snatch" (al-khatf) means to seize quickly. "The people" refers to the polytheists of Quraysh. It is also said that it refers to Persia and the Romans. The phrase ﴿and gave you refuge﴾ (فَآواكم): it is said "āwā ilayhi" (آوى إليه), with both the long and short vowel forms, meaning "he joined himself to him." So the meaning is that Allah joined you to Madinah, or to the Ansar. ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾ means He gave you strength through victory in the battlefields, among which is the Day of Badr, or He strengthened you with the angels on the Day of Badr. ﴿And provided you with good things﴾, among which are the spoils of war, ﴿so that you may be grateful﴾, that is, in hope that you would give thanks for these blessings which He bestowed upon you.

The word al-khawn (الخَوْنُ), as in al-Kashshaf, originally means deficiency, just as al-wafa' (الوَفاءُ) means completeness. Then it was used for the opposite of trustworthiness and fulfilment, because when you betray a man in something, you have brought deficiency upon him. It is also said its meaning is treachery and concealing something. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾ (Ghafir: 19). Allah forbade them to betray Him by abandoning any of what He made obligatory upon them, or to betray His Messenger by abandoning anything of what He entrusted them with, or by abandoning anything of what he prescribed for them, or to betray any of the trusts (al-amanat, الأماناتِ) with which they were entrusted. They are called trusts (amanat) because security (al-amn) is felt through them from withholding what is due, and the word is derived from al-amn. The clause ﴿while you know﴾ (وأنتم تعلمون) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). That is: while you know that such an act is betrayal, and so you commit betrayal deliberately. Or it means: you are of the people of knowledge, not of the people of ignorance.

Then He said: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾, because they are a cause of falling into many sins. Thus they become, in this respect, a test by which Allah examines His servants. Although, from another respect, they are the adornment of the worldly life, as in the other verse: ﴿and that with Allah is a great reward﴾. So prefer His right over your wealth and children, so that there may be attained for you what He has of the aforementioned reward.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿And remember when you were few﴾, he said: This tribe of the Arabs was the most humiliated of people in humiliation, the most miserable in life, the most hungry in their bellies, the most naked in their skins, and the most manifest in misguidance. Whoever lived among them lived in misery, and whoever died among them was cast into the Fire. They were eaten and did not eat. By Allah, we know of no tribe among the inhabitants of the earth at that time that was in a worse state than them, until Allah brought Islam, and He established them in the lands, expanded provision for them, and made them kings over the necks of the people. Through Islam, Allah gave what you have seen. So be thankful to Allah for His blessings, for your Lord is a Bestower who loves gratitude, and those who are grateful are in increase from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His words ﴿that the people may snatch you away﴾, he said: in the Jahiliyyah, in Makkah; ﴿and gave you refuge﴾ means to Islam.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Wahb concerning His words ﴿that the people may snatch you away﴾, he said: the people at that time were Persia and the Romans.

Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Nu'aym and al-Daylami in Musnad al-Firdaws related from Ibn Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning His words: ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that the people would snatch you away.﴾ It was said: O Messenger of Allah, who are the people? He said: "The people of Persia."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi concerning His words "and gave you refuge": he said, to the Ansar in Madinah. ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾: he said, on the Day of Badr.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Jabir ibn Abd Allah that "Abu Sufyan went out from Makkah, and Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Abu Sufyan is at such and such a place.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Abu Sufyan is at such and such a place, so go out to him secretly.' A man from the hypocrites wrote to Abu Sufyan: 'Muhammad intends to attack you, so take your precaution.' So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not betray Allah and the Messenger﴾, the verse."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abd Allah ibn Abi Qatadah, who said: This verse ﴿Do not betray Allah and the Messenger﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah ibn Abd al-Mundhir. They asked him on the day of Qurayzah, "What is this matter?" He pointed to his throat, that it was slaughter. So it was revealed.

Abu Lubabah said: "My feet did not move until I knew that I had betrayed Allah and His Messenger."

Sunayd and Ibn Jarir related from al-Zuhri something similar, but longer than it.

Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Kalbi that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abu Lubabah to Qurayzah, and he was an ally of theirs. So he gestured with his hand that it was slaughter, and so it was revealed."

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi concerning this verse that it was revealed concerning Abu Lubabah, and that it was abrogated (nasakhat, نَسَخَتْها) by the verse in Bara'ah (al-Tawbah): ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾ (al-Tawbah: 102).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas concerning His words ﴿Do not betray Allah﴾: by abandoning His obligations; ﴿and the Messenger﴾: by abandoning his sunan (practices) and committing what he forbade; ﴿or betray your trusts﴾: he said, do not diminish them. The trust (al-amanah) is the deeds with which Allah entrusted the servants.

Ibn Jarir related from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah who said: This verse was revealed concerning the killing of Uthman. Perhaps his meaning is that the killing of Uthman is among what falls under its generality.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Yazid ibn Abi Habib concerning the verse, he said: it is neglecting weapons in the military campaigns. Perhaps his meaning is that this falls under its generality.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Mas'ud who said: There is none of you but that he contains a trial, for Allah says: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾. So whoever among you seeks refuge, let him seek refuge in Allah from the misleading trials.

Those same narrators related from Ibn Zayd concerning the verse, he said: The trial is the trial of testing; He tested them, and he recited: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ (al-Anbiya': 35).

He, glory be to Him, made taqwa (God-consciousness, i.e. guarding against disobeying His commands and falling into what He has forbidden) a condition for the granting mentioned, while knowing in advance whether they would be God-conscious or not, in keeping with the way people address one another. Al-Furqan is that by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. The meaning is that He will grant them, in steadiness of hearts, sharpness of insight and good guidance, that by which they can tell the two apart when things become confused.

It has also been said: al-Furqan is the way out of doubts and deliverance from everything they fear. From this is the saying of the poet:

"What is there for you, from prolonged grief, but furqan, after the companions have departed and gone away?"

And from this is the saying of another:

"How can I hope for eternity when death is seeking me, and I have no furqan from the cup of death?"

al-Farra' said: the intended meaning of al-Furqan is victory and help.

Ibn Ishaq said: al-Furqan is the separation between truth and falsehood, and Ibn Zayd said the same.

al-Suddi said: al-Furqan is deliverance.

The interpretation of al-Furqan as a way out and deliverance is supported by His saying, exalted is He: "And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out" (al-Talaq 65:2). This was also the view of Mujahid and Malik ibn Anas.

"And He will remove from you your misdeeds" means He will cover them so that they are not apparent, "and forgive you" what you have committed of sins. It has been said that the misdeeds (sayyi'at) refer to minor sins, and the sins that are forgiven refer to major sins. It has also been said that the meaning is that He will forgive them what preceded and what followed of their sins. "And Allah is the Owner of great bounty": He is the one who bestows favour upon His servants by covering misdeeds and forgiving sins.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying "He will grant you a furqan," that he said: it is the way out.

Ibn Jarir also transmitted from him that he said: it is deliverance.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ikrimah the same as this.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said: it is victory.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verses 30–33:

His saying: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is governed by a verb omitted from the text, meaning: "And remember, O Muhammad, the time when the disbelievers plotted against you." Or it is coordinated with what preceded in His saying ﴿And remember﴾. God reminds His Messenger of this great blessing which He bestowed upon him, namely his deliverance from the plotting and scheming of the disbelievers, as its explanation will come. ﴿That they might confine you﴾: "they might confine you" by wounding, as Tha'lab and Abu Hatim and others said, and from it is the saying of the poet:

﴿Then I said: "Woe to you! What is in your document?" They said: "The Caliph has become afflicted, sick and wounded."﴾

It was also said that the meaning is "to imprison you," as one says athbatahu when he detains him. It was also said: "to bind you fast," and from it is: ﴿Then tie the bonds tightly﴾ (Muhammad: 4).

Al-Sha'bi read: "liyubayyitūka" from al-bayt (to attack by night), and it was also read "liyuthabbitūka" with a shaddah.

﴿Or expel you﴾ is coordinated with what came before it: that is, they would expel you from Makkah, which is your city and the city of your family. The clause ﴿And they plot, and God plots﴾ is a new (resumptive) sentence. Makr (plotting) means arranging a matter in secrecy. The meaning is that they conceal what they prepare against the Messenger of God ﹣ﷺ﹣ of schemes, and God requites them for that and turns their scheming back upon their own necks. What comes from Him, exalted is He, is called makr by way of mushakalah (correspondence of wording), as in its parallels. ﴿And God is the best of planners﴾: that is, the one who requites the planners for their plotting with the like of their action. So He punishes them for their plotting from where they do not perceive, and this becomes more harmful to them and a greater affliction than their plotting.

His saying: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾: that is, those that come to them and that you recite to them, they say, out of obstinacy, defiance and distance from the truth: ﴿We have indeed heard﴾ what you recite to us. ﴿If we wished, we could say the like of this﴾ which you have recited to us. It was said: they said this out of a delusion that they were capable of that. When they tried to say the like of it, they were unable to do so, and then they said, out of stubbornness and defiance: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾: that is, what the copyists write down of the reports of the ancients. Its explanation has already been given in full.

﴿And when they said﴾: that is, remember when they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ — with the word "al-haqq" in the accusative as the predicate of kāna, and the pronoun being a separator (fasl); it is also permissible to read it in the nominative. Al-Zajjaj said: "I know of no one who read it that way, and there is no disagreement among the grammarians about its permissibility. But recitation is a sunnah (transmitted practice)." The meaning is: if the Qur'an that Muhammad brought us is the truth, ﴿then rain down on us﴾. They said this statement as an exaggeration in denial and rejection.

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said amtara in punishment and matara in mercy. And in al-Kashshaf: the use of imṭār in the sense of punishment is frequent.

﴿Or bring us a painful punishment﴾: they asked to be punished by being stoned with stones from the sky, or by other kinds of severe punishment.

God answered them with His saying: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you [O Muhammad] are among them﴾, for as long as you are among them, they are in a respite from the punishment, which is annihilation (al-isti'sal). ﴿Nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾.

It is reported that they used to say in the circumambulation: "Ghufrānaka" (Your forgiveness). That is: God would not punish them while they are seeking forgiveness. It was also said: the meaning is, if they were among those who believe in God and seek His forgiveness, He would not punish them. It was also said: the seeking of forgiveness refers to the Muslims who were among them; that is, God would not punish them while among them are those of the Muslims who seek forgiveness. When those [Muslims] left from among them, He punished them on the day of Badr and after it. It was also said: the meaning is: God would not punish them while in their loins there is one who seeks forgiveness from God.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, and al-Khatib reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾, that he said: "Quraysh consulted one night in Makkah. Some of them said: 'When he rises in the morning, bind him in chains' — they meant the Prophet ﷺ. Others said: 'Rather, kill him.' Others said: 'Rather, expel him.' So God informed His Prophet of that, and ʿAli slept on the bed of the Prophet ﷺ until he joined the cave. When they woke, they rushed at him, and when they saw that it was ʿAli, God turned back their plot. They said: 'Where is your companion?' He said: 'I do not know.' So they tracked his trail, and when they reached the mountain it became confused for them, so they climbed the mountain and passed by the cave, and they saw spider's web at its entrance, and they said: 'If he had entered here, there would not be spider's web at its door.' So he remained in it for three nights."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, mentioning the story at greater length than what is here. In it is mention of the old man of Najd, that is Iblis, and his advice to them when they gathered in Dar al-Nadwa for consultation about the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, and that Abu Jahl suggested they take one youth from each tribe of Quraysh and give each of them a sword, then they would strike him with a single blow, so that when they killed him his blood would be scattered among the tribes. The old man of Najd said: "By God, this is the opinion," and so they dispersed upon that.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr who said: "When they plotted against the Prophet ﷺ to imprison him, or kill him, or expel him, his paternal uncle Abu Talib said to him: 'Do you know what they have plotted against you?' He said: 'They want to imprison me, or kill me, or expel me.' He said: 'Who told you this?' He said: 'My Lord.' He said: 'How excellent a Lord is your Lord! Advise Him well (istawṣi bihi khayran).' He said: 'Am I the one who should advise Him? Rather, He advises me.'"

Ibn Jarir also reported it through another chain from him, but this is not sound, for Abu Talib had died some years before the time of the Hijrah.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾, he said: "﴿That they might confine you﴾ means that they might bind you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ killed ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt, Tuʿayma ibn ʿAdi, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith on the day of Badr by way of sabr (execution by holding captive). al-Miqdad had taken al-Nadr captive, and when he was ordered to be killed, al-Miqdad said: 'O Messenger of God, my captive!' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'He used to say in the Book of God what he used to say.' He said: 'And concerning him this verse was revealed: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾.'" This is a mursal report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Anas ibn Malik who said: "Abu Jahl ibn Hisham said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ — the verse — so there was revealed: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding the verse, that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir reported from ʿAta' something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The polytheists used to circumambulate the House and say: 'Labbayka Allahumma labbayk, la sharika laka illa sharikan huwa laka, tamlikuhu wa ma malak' (Here I am, O Allah, here I am; You have no partner except a partner who is Yours: You own him and what he owns). And they would say: 'Ghufranaka, ghufranaka' (Your forgiveness). So God revealed: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "There were two securities among them: the Prophet ﷺ and the seeking of forgiveness. The Prophet ﷺ departed, and the seeking of forgiveness remained."

al-Tirmidhi reported, and graded it weak, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "God sent down to me two securities for my community: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse. So when I pass away, I shall leave among them the seeking of forgiveness."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Abu Hurayra who said: "Among you there were two securities; one has passed and the other remains," and he recited: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim, and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari something similar too. The hadiths from the Messenger of God ﷺ concerning seeking forgiveness in general are very numerous and well known in the books of hadith.
