ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ahmad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, and al-Khatib reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾, that he said: "Quraysh consulted one night in Makkah. Some of them said: 'When he rises in the morning, bind him in chains' — they meant the Prophet ﷺ. Others said: 'Rather, kill him.' Others said: 'Rather, expel him.' So God informed His Prophet of that, and ʿAli slept on the bed of the Prophet ﷺ until he joined the cave. When they woke, they rushed at him, and when they saw that it was ʿAli, God turned back their plot. They said: 'Where is your companion?' He said: 'I do not know.' So they tracked his trail, and when they reached the mountain it became confused for them, so they climbed the mountain and passed by the cave, and they saw spider's web at its entrance, and they said: 'If he had entered here, there would not be spider's web at its door.' So he remained in it for three nights."

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, mentioning the story at greater length than what is here. In it is mention of the old man of Najd, that is Iblis, and his advice to them when they gathered in Dar al-Nadwa for consultation about the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, and that Abu Jahl suggested they take one youth from each tribe of Quraysh and give each of them a sword, then they would strike him with a single blow, so that when they killed him his blood would be scattered among the tribes. The old man of Najd said: "By God, this is the opinion," and so they dispersed upon that.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr who said: "When they plotted against the Prophet ﷺ to imprison him, or kill him, or expel him, his paternal uncle Abu Talib said to him: 'Do you know what they have plotted against you?' He said: 'They want to imprison me, or kill me, or expel me.' He said: 'Who told you this?' He said: 'My Lord.' He said: 'How excellent a Lord is your Lord! Advise Him well (istawṣi bihi khayran).' He said: 'Am I the one who should advise Him? Rather, He advises me.'"

Ibn Jarir also reported it through another chain from him, but this is not sound, for Abu Talib had died some years before the time of the Hijrah.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding His saying: ﴿And when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾, he said: "﴿That they might confine you﴾ means that they might bind you."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ killed ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt, Tuʿayma ibn ʿAdi, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith on the day of Badr by way of sabr (execution by holding captive). al-Miqdad had taken al-Nadr captive, and when he was ordered to be killed, al-Miqdad said: 'O Messenger of God, my captive!' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'He used to say in the Book of God what he used to say.' He said: 'And concerning him this verse was revealed: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾.'" This is a mursal report.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Anas ibn Malik who said: "Abu Jahl ibn Hisham said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ — the verse — so there was revealed: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from Qatada that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding the verse, that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir reported from ʿAta' something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The polytheists used to circumambulate the House and say: 'Labbayka Allahumma labbayk, la sharika laka illa sharikan huwa laka, tamlikuhu wa ma malak' (Here I am, O Allah, here I am; You have no partner except a partner who is Yours: You own him and what he owns). And they would say: 'Ghufranaka, ghufranaka' (Your forgiveness). So God revealed: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "There were two securities among them: the Prophet ﷺ and the seeking of forgiveness. The Prophet ﷺ departed, and the seeking of forgiveness remained."

al-Tirmidhi reported, and graded it weak, from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "God sent down to me two securities for my community: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse. So when I pass away, I shall leave among them the seeking of forgiveness."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Abu Hurayra who said: "Among you there were two securities; one has passed and the other remains," and he recited: ﴿But Allah would not punish them﴾ — the verse.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim, and Ibn ʿAsakir reported from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari something similar too. The hadiths from the Messenger of God ﷺ concerning seeking forgiveness in general are very numerous and well known in the books of hadith.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verses 30–33:

His saying: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is governed by a verb omitted from the text, meaning: "And remember, O Muhammad, the time when the disbelievers plotted against you." Or it is coordinated with what preceded in His saying ﴿And remember﴾. God reminds His Messenger of this great blessing which He bestowed upon him, namely his deliverance from the plotting and scheming of the disbelievers, as its explanation will come. ﴿That they might confine you﴾: "they might confine you" by wounding, as Tha'lab and Abu Hatim and others said, and from it is the saying of the poet:

﴿Then I said: "Woe to you! What is in your document?" They said: "The Caliph has become afflicted, sick and wounded."﴾

It was also said that the meaning is "to imprison you," as one says athbatahu when he detains him. It was also said: "to bind you fast," and from it is: ﴿Then tie the bonds tightly﴾ (Muhammad: 4).

Al-Sha'bi read: "liyubayyitūka" from al-bayt (to attack by night), and it was also read "liyuthabbitūka" with a shaddah.

﴿Or expel you﴾ is coordinated with what came before it: that is, they would expel you from Makkah, which is your city and the city of your family. The clause ﴿And they plot, and God plots﴾ is a new (resumptive) sentence. Makr (plotting) means arranging a matter in secrecy. The meaning is that they conceal what they prepare against the Messenger of God ﹣ﷺ﹣ of schemes, and God requites them for that and turns their scheming back upon their own necks. What comes from Him, exalted is He, is called makr by way of mushakalah (correspondence of wording), as in its parallels. ﴿And God is the best of planners﴾: that is, the one who requites the planners for their plotting with the like of their action. So He punishes them for their plotting from where they do not perceive, and this becomes more harmful to them and a greater affliction than their plotting.

His saying: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾: that is, those that come to them and that you recite to them, they say, out of obstinacy, defiance and distance from the truth: ﴿We have indeed heard﴾ what you recite to us. ﴿If we wished, we could say the like of this﴾ which you have recited to us. It was said: they said this out of a delusion that they were capable of that. When they tried to say the like of it, they were unable to do so, and then they said, out of stubbornness and defiance: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾: that is, what the copyists write down of the reports of the ancients. Its explanation has already been given in full.

﴿And when they said﴾: that is, remember when they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You﴾ — with the word "al-haqq" in the accusative as the predicate of kāna, and the pronoun being a separator (fasl); it is also permissible to read it in the nominative. Al-Zajjaj said: "I know of no one who read it that way, and there is no disagreement among the grammarians about its permissibility. But recitation is a sunnah (transmitted practice)." The meaning is: if the Qur'an that Muhammad brought us is the truth, ﴿then rain down on us﴾. They said this statement as an exaggeration in denial and rejection.

Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said amtara in punishment and matara in mercy. And in al-Kashshaf: the use of imṭār in the sense of punishment is frequent.

﴿Or bring us a painful punishment﴾: they asked to be punished by being stoned with stones from the sky, or by other kinds of severe punishment.

God answered them with His saying: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you [O Muhammad] are among them﴾, for as long as you are among them, they are in a respite from the punishment, which is annihilation (al-isti'sal). ﴿Nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾.

It is reported that they used to say in the circumambulation: "Ghufrānaka" (Your forgiveness). That is: God would not punish them while they are seeking forgiveness. It was also said: the meaning is, if they were among those who believe in God and seek His forgiveness, He would not punish them. It was also said: the seeking of forgiveness refers to the Muslims who were among them; that is, God would not punish them while among them are those of the Muslims who seek forgiveness. When those [Muslims] left from among them, He punished them on the day of Badr and after it. It was also said: the meaning is: God would not punish them while in their loins there is one who seeks forgiveness from God.

He (glorified is He) explained that what prevents their punishment is the two matters mentioned earlier: the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them, and the seeking of forgiveness. Then he mentioned that these disbelievers, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, deserve God's punishment for the vile deeds they committed.

The meaning is: What is there for them that would prevent their punishment? Al-Akhfash said: The particle *an* (أنْ) is superfluous.

Al-Nahhas said: If it were as he said, it would make *yu'adhdhibahum* (يُعَذِّبَهم) nominative. The clause ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): that is, "And what prevents their punishment, while they bar people from the Sacred Mosque?" This happened in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, when they prevented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions from the House. The clause ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause referring to the subject of *yasuddūn* (يَصُدُّونَ). This is a refutation of their claim that they are the custodians of the House and that its affairs are entrusted to them. Then he said, clarifying who has that right: ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾, meaning: His protectors are only those who are among the God-fearing, who avoid polytheism and sins. ﴿ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (but most of them do not know this). Passing judgement on the majority as ignorant implies that a minority do know, but they are obstinate.

Regarding ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾: *al-mukā'* (المُكاءُ) means whistling, from *makā yamkū mukāan*, and from it is the verse of ʿAntarah:

*And a friend of a flirtatious woman, I left him slain, his diaphragm whistling like the cut of al-Aʿlam's jaw.*

That is, it makes a sound. From it comes *makat ist al-dābbah* (مَكَتِ اسْتُ الدّابَّةِ), when the animal's rear expels wind. It is said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird in the Hijaz called *al-mukkā'*. A poet said:

*When the mukkā' sings in a place without foliage, woe to the people of sheep and donkeys.*

*Al-tasdiyah* (التَّصْدِيَةُ) means clapping. One says *ṣadda yuṣaddī tasdiyatan* when he claps. From it is the saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Iṭnābah:

*They all remained, with an uproar for them, a whistling by the House, with clapping.*

That is, with clapping. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is striking with the hands, and *al-tasdiyah* is shouting. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling. It is also said: *al-tasdiyah* is their preventing people from the House. It is said that the original form on this view is *tasdidah*, and one of the two *dāl*s was changed into a *yā'*.

The meaning of the verse is that the polytheists used to whistle and clap at the House, which is the place of prayer and worship. They put that in place of prayer, intending thereby to distract the Muslims who were praying. It has been recited with the accusative *ṣalātahum* (صَلاتَهم) as the predicate of *kāna* (كانَ), with what follows it as its subject.

Regarding ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾: this is a shift to addressing the disbelievers, as a threat to them and to intensify terror in their hearts. What is meant is the punishment of this world, such as on the day of Badr, and the punishment of the Hereafter.

Regarding ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾: when He (glorified is He) finished describing the states of these disbelievers in bodily acts of obedience, He followed it with describing their states in financial acts of obedience.

The meaning is: the aim of these disbelievers in spending their wealth is to bar people from the path of truth by fighting the Messenger of God (ﷺ), gathering armies for that, and spending their wealth on them. This is what happened from the Quraysh disbelievers on the day of Badr, the day of Uhud, and the day of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), for the leaders used to spend their wealth on the army. Then God (glorified is He) informed about the unseen in a miraculous manner, saying: ﴿فَسَيُنْفِقُونَها﴾ (so they will spend it), meaning this spending will take place from them, and then the outcome of that will be that their spending becomes a regret for them. It is as if the wealth itself turns into regret, becoming remorse. Then, in the end, they will be overcome, as God promised in verses such as His saying: ﴿كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَأغْلِبَنَّ أنا ورُسُلِي﴾ (Al-Mujadila: 21).

The meaning of *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") in both places is either a delay in time, referring to the distance between the aforementioned spending and the emergence of the state of Islam, or a delay in rank, referring to the gap between giving up wealth and the non-attainment of the goal, which is the total opposite of it. Then He said: ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾, meaning they persisted in disbelief. This is because among those disbelievers mentioned earlier were some who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. That is, they are driven toward it and not toward anything else.

Then He explained the reason for which He did to them what He did, saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ﴾, meaning the wicked group of disbelievers from the good group, who are the believers. ﴿ويَجْعَلَ الخَبِيثَ بَعْضَهُ عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾, meaning He makes the wicked group of disbelievers piled upon one another. ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ is an expression for gathering and joining: that is, He gathers some of them upon others and joins some of them to others, until they heap up because of their extreme crowding. One says *rakama al-shay' yarkumuhu* when he gathers it and places some of it upon other parts. The indication of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to the wicked group, ﴿هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾, meaning those who are complete in loss. It has also been said: *al-khabīth* (الخَبِيثُ) and *al-ṭayyib* (الطَّيِّبُ) are attributes of wealth, and the sense is: He separates the wicked wealth that the polytheists spent from the good wealth that the Muslims spent, then He gathers those wicked wealths upon one another, casting them into Hell and punishing them with them, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿فَتُكْوى بِها جِباهُهم وجُنُوبُهم وظُهُورُهم﴾ (At-Tawbah: 35).

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The *lām* (لام) on this view is related to His saying ﴿ثُمَّ تَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ حَسْرَةً﴾, and on the first view it is related to *yuḥsharūn* (يُحْشَرُونَ). The indicator ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to those who disbelieved. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهم وهم يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ﴾, then He excepted the people of polytheism, saying: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾, that he said: Their punishment is the conquest of Makkah.

Ibn Ishaq and Abu Hatim narrated from ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ while they deny the signs of God and deny His messengers.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾: that is, whoever believes in God and worships Him, you and whoever follows you. ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾: those who leave it and establish prayer at it, that is, you and whoever believes in you.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾ that he said: Those who are wherever they are.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: The Quraysh used to oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) during the circumambulation, mocking, whistling and clapping. Then this was revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Quraysh used to circumambulate the Kaʿbah naked, whistling and clapping. So God revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. He said: *al-mukā'* is whistling; they were only likened to the whistling of birds. "*Tasdiyah*" is clapping. And God revealed about them: ﴿قُلْ مَن حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Aʿraf: 32), the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated similar to this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated similar to this from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: *al-mukā'* is whistling, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling; they mix all of that together, mixing their prayer before Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird called *al-mukkā'*, found in the land of the Hijaz, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying "*illā mukkā'an*" (إلّا مُكّاءً): he said: They used to interlace their fingers and whistle through them. "*Wa tasdiyatan*" (وتَصْدِيَةً): he said: their hindering of people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: The polytheists used to circumambulate the House keeping it on their left. This is His saying: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. So *al-mukā'* is like the blowing of a horn, and *al-tasdiyah* is their circumambulating it on the left.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His saying ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ that he said: It means the people of Badr. God punished them with killing and capture.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalā'il* all narrated through his chain: He said: al-Zuhri, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatadah and al-Husayn ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAmr told me, saying: When the Quraysh were struck on the day of Badr and their remnant returned to Makkah, and Abu Sufyan returned with his caravan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Rabiʿah, ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Safwan ibn Umayyah walked, with men from the Quraysh whose fathers and sons had been struck. They spoke to Abu Sufyan and to those among the Quraysh who had trade in that caravan, and said: O assembly of the Quraysh, Muhammad has wronged you and killed your best men. So support war against him with this wealth, so that perhaps we may take revenge from him. They did so. Concerning them, as Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned, God revealed: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ up to ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: This verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similar to this from Mujahid.

These and others narrated similar to this from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hakam ibn ʿUtaybah regarding the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who spent forty *ūqiyyah* of gold on the polytheists of the Quraysh on the day of Uhud. The *ūqiyyah* at that time was forty-two *mithqāl* of gold.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shimr ibn ʿAtiyyah regarding His saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ﴾, that he said: On the Day of Resurrection He will separate whatever good deeds were done in the world; then the entire world will be taken and cast into Hell.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ that he said: He gathers it all together.

He (glorified is He) explained that what prevents their punishment is the two matters mentioned earlier: the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them, and the seeking of forgiveness. Then he mentioned that these disbelievers, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, deserve God's punishment for the vile deeds they committed.

The meaning is: What is there for them that would prevent their punishment? Al-Akhfash said: The particle *an* (أنْ) is superfluous.

Al-Nahhas said: If it were as he said, it would make *yu'adhdhibahum* (يُعَذِّبَهم) nominative. The clause ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): that is, "And what prevents their punishment, while they bar people from the Sacred Mosque?" This happened in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, when they prevented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions from the House. The clause ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause referring to the subject of *yasuddūn* (يَصُدُّونَ). This is a refutation of their claim that they are the custodians of the House and that its affairs are entrusted to them. Then he said, clarifying who has that right: ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾, meaning: His protectors are only those who are among the God-fearing, who avoid polytheism and sins. ﴿ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (but most of them do not know this). Passing judgement on the majority as ignorant implies that a minority do know, but they are obstinate.

Regarding ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾: *al-mukā'* (المُكاءُ) means whistling, from *makā yamkū mukāan*, and from it is the verse of ʿAntarah:

*And a friend of a flirtatious woman, I left him slain, his diaphragm whistling like the cut of al-Aʿlam's jaw.*

That is, it makes a sound. From it comes *makat ist al-dābbah* (مَكَتِ اسْتُ الدّابَّةِ), when the animal's rear expels wind. It is said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird in the Hijaz called *al-mukkā'*. A poet said:

*When the mukkā' sings in a place without foliage, woe to the people of sheep and donkeys.*

*Al-tasdiyah* (التَّصْدِيَةُ) means clapping. One says *ṣadda yuṣaddī tasdiyatan* when he claps. From it is the saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Iṭnābah:

*They all remained, with an uproar for them, a whistling by the House, with clapping.*

That is, with clapping. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is striking with the hands, and *al-tasdiyah* is shouting. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling. It is also said: *al-tasdiyah* is their preventing people from the House. It is said that the original form on this view is *tasdidah*, and one of the two *dāl*s was changed into a *yā'*.

The meaning of the verse is that the polytheists used to whistle and clap at the House, which is the place of prayer and worship. They put that in place of prayer, intending thereby to distract the Muslims who were praying. It has been recited with the accusative *ṣalātahum* (صَلاتَهم) as the predicate of *kāna* (كانَ), with what follows it as its subject.

Regarding ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾: this is a shift to addressing the disbelievers, as a threat to them and to intensify terror in their hearts. What is meant is the punishment of this world, such as on the day of Badr, and the punishment of the Hereafter.

Regarding ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾: when He (glorified is He) finished describing the states of these disbelievers in bodily acts of obedience, He followed it with describing their states in financial acts of obedience.

The meaning is: the aim of these disbelievers in spending their wealth is to bar people from the path of truth by fighting the Messenger of God (ﷺ), gathering armies for that, and spending their wealth on them. This is what happened from the Quraysh disbelievers on the day of Badr, the day of Uhud, and the day of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), for the leaders used to spend their wealth on the army. Then God (glorified is He) informed about the unseen in a miraculous manner, saying: ﴿فَسَيُنْفِقُونَها﴾ (so they will spend it), meaning this spending will take place from them, and then the outcome of that will be that their spending becomes a regret for them. It is as if the wealth itself turns into regret, becoming remorse. Then, in the end, they will be overcome, as God promised in verses such as His saying: ﴿كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَأغْلِبَنَّ أنا ورُسُلِي﴾ (Al-Mujadila: 21).

The meaning of *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") in both places is either a delay in time, referring to the distance between the aforementioned spending and the emergence of the state of Islam, or a delay in rank, referring to the gap between giving up wealth and the non-attainment of the goal, which is the total opposite of it. Then He said: ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾, meaning they persisted in disbelief. This is because among those disbelievers mentioned earlier were some who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. That is, they are driven toward it and not toward anything else.

Then He explained the reason for which He did to them what He did, saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ﴾, meaning the wicked group of disbelievers from the good group, who are the believers. ﴿ويَجْعَلَ الخَبِيثَ بَعْضَهُ عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾, meaning He makes the wicked group of disbelievers piled upon one another. ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ is an expression for gathering and joining: that is, He gathers some of them upon others and joins some of them to others, until they heap up because of their extreme crowding. One says *rakama al-shay' yarkumuhu* when he gathers it and places some of it upon other parts. The indication of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to the wicked group, ﴿هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾, meaning those who are complete in loss. It has also been said: *al-khabīth* (الخَبِيثُ) and *al-ṭayyib* (الطَّيِّبُ) are attributes of wealth, and the sense is: He separates the wicked wealth that the polytheists spent from the good wealth that the Muslims spent, then He gathers those wicked wealths upon one another, casting them into Hell and punishing them with them, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿فَتُكْوى بِها جِباهُهم وجُنُوبُهم وظُهُورُهم﴾ (At-Tawbah: 35).

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The *lām* (لام) on this view is related to His saying ﴿ثُمَّ تَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ حَسْرَةً﴾, and on the first view it is related to *yuḥsharūn* (يُحْشَرُونَ). The indicator ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to those who disbelieved. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهم وهم يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ﴾, then He excepted the people of polytheism, saying: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾, that he said: Their punishment is the conquest of Makkah.

Ibn Ishaq and Abu Hatim narrated from ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ while they deny the signs of God and deny His messengers.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾: that is, whoever believes in God and worships Him, you and whoever follows you. ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾: those who leave it and establish prayer at it, that is, you and whoever believes in you.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾ that he said: Those who are wherever they are.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: The Quraysh used to oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) during the circumambulation, mocking, whistling and clapping. Then this was revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Quraysh used to circumambulate the Kaʿbah naked, whistling and clapping. So God revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. He said: *al-mukā'* is whistling; they were only likened to the whistling of birds. "*Tasdiyah*" is clapping. And God revealed about them: ﴿قُلْ مَن حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Aʿraf: 32), the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated similar to this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated similar to this from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: *al-mukā'* is whistling, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling; they mix all of that together, mixing their prayer before Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird called *al-mukkā'*, found in the land of the Hijaz, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying "*illā mukkā'an*" (إلّا مُكّاءً): he said: They used to interlace their fingers and whistle through them. "*Wa tasdiyatan*" (وتَصْدِيَةً): he said: their hindering of people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: The polytheists used to circumambulate the House keeping it on their left. This is His saying: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. So *al-mukā'* is like the blowing of a horn, and *al-tasdiyah* is their circumambulating it on the left.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His saying ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ that he said: It means the people of Badr. God punished them with killing and capture.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalā'il* all narrated through his chain: He said: al-Zuhri, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatadah and al-Husayn ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAmr told me, saying: When the Quraysh were struck on the day of Badr and their remnant returned to Makkah, and Abu Sufyan returned with his caravan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Rabiʿah, ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Safwan ibn Umayyah walked, with men from the Quraysh whose fathers and sons had been struck. They spoke to Abu Sufyan and to those among the Quraysh who had trade in that caravan, and said: O assembly of the Quraysh, Muhammad has wronged you and killed your best men. So support war against him with this wealth, so that perhaps we may take revenge from him. They did so. Concerning them, as Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned, God revealed: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ up to ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: This verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similar to this from Mujahid.

These and others narrated similar to this from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hakam ibn ʿUtaybah regarding the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who spent forty *ūqiyyah* of gold on the polytheists of the Quraysh on the day of Uhud. The *ūqiyyah* at that time was forty-two *mithqāl* of gold.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shimr ibn ʿAtiyyah regarding His saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ﴾, that he said: On the Day of Resurrection He will separate whatever good deeds were done in the world; then the entire world will be taken and cast into Hell.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ that he said: He gathers it all together.

He (glorified is He) explained that what prevents their punishment is the two matters mentioned earlier: the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them, and the seeking of forgiveness. Then he mentioned that these disbelievers, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, deserve God's punishment for the vile deeds they committed.

The meaning is: What is there for them that would prevent their punishment? Al-Akhfash said: The particle *an* (أنْ) is superfluous.

Al-Nahhas said: If it were as he said, it would make *yu'adhdhibahum* (يُعَذِّبَهم) nominative. The clause ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): that is, "And what prevents their punishment, while they bar people from the Sacred Mosque?" This happened in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, when they prevented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions from the House. The clause ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause referring to the subject of *yasuddūn* (يَصُدُّونَ). This is a refutation of their claim that they are the custodians of the House and that its affairs are entrusted to them. Then he said, clarifying who has that right: ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾, meaning: His protectors are only those who are among the God-fearing, who avoid polytheism and sins. ﴿ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (but most of them do not know this). Passing judgement on the majority as ignorant implies that a minority do know, but they are obstinate.

Regarding ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾: *al-mukā'* (المُكاءُ) means whistling, from *makā yamkū mukāan*, and from it is the verse of ʿAntarah:

*And a friend of a flirtatious woman, I left him slain, his diaphragm whistling like the cut of al-Aʿlam's jaw.*

That is, it makes a sound. From it comes *makat ist al-dābbah* (مَكَتِ اسْتُ الدّابَّةِ), when the animal's rear expels wind. It is said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird in the Hijaz called *al-mukkā'*. A poet said:

*When the mukkā' sings in a place without foliage, woe to the people of sheep and donkeys.*

*Al-tasdiyah* (التَّصْدِيَةُ) means clapping. One says *ṣadda yuṣaddī tasdiyatan* when he claps. From it is the saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Iṭnābah:

*They all remained, with an uproar for them, a whistling by the House, with clapping.*

That is, with clapping. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is striking with the hands, and *al-tasdiyah* is shouting. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling. It is also said: *al-tasdiyah* is their preventing people from the House. It is said that the original form on this view is *tasdidah*, and one of the two *dāl*s was changed into a *yā'*.

They put that in place of prayer, intending thereby to distract the Muslims who were praying. It has been recited with the accusative *ṣalātahum* (صَلاتَهم) as the predicate of *kāna* (كانَ), with what follows it as its subject.

Regarding ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾: this is a shift to addressing the disbelievers, as a threat to them and to intensify terror in their hearts. What is meant is the punishment of this world, such as on the day of Badr, and the punishment of the Hereafter.

Regarding ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾: when He (glorified is He) finished describing the states of these disbelievers in bodily acts of obedience, He followed it with describing their states in financial acts of obedience.

The meaning is: the aim of these disbelievers in spending their wealth is to bar people from the path of truth by fighting the Messenger of God (ﷺ), gathering armies for that, and spending their wealth on them. This is what happened from the Quraysh disbelievers on the day of Badr, the day of Uhud, and the day of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), for the leaders used to spend their wealth on the army. Then God (glorified is He) informed about the unseen in a miraculous manner, saying: ﴿فَسَيُنْفِقُونَها﴾ (so they will spend it), meaning this spending will take place from them, and then the outcome of that will be that their spending becomes a regret for them. It is as if the wealth itself turns into regret, becoming remorse. Then, in the end, they will be overcome, as God promised in verses such as His saying: ﴿كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَأغْلِبَنَّ أنا ورُسُلِي﴾ (Al-Mujadila: 21).

The meaning of *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") in both places is either a delay in time, referring to the distance between the aforementioned spending and the emergence of the state of Islam, or a delay in rank, referring to the gap between giving up wealth and the non-attainment of the goal, which is the total opposite of it. Then He said: ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾, meaning they persisted in disbelief. This is because among those disbelievers mentioned earlier were some who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. That is, they are driven toward it and not toward anything else.

Then He explained the reason for which He did to them what He did, saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ﴾, meaning the wicked group of disbelievers from the good group, who are the believers. ﴿ويَجْعَلَ الخَبِيثَ بَعْضَهُ عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾, meaning He makes the wicked group of disbelievers piled upon one another. ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ is an expression for gathering and joining: that is, He gathers some of them upon others and joins some of them to others, until they heap up because of their extreme crowding. One says *rakama al-shay' yarkumuhu* when he gathers it and places some of it upon other parts. The indication of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to the wicked group, ﴿هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾, meaning those who are complete in loss. It has also been said: *al-khabīth* (الخَبِيثُ) and *al-ṭayyib* (الطَّيِّبُ) are attributes of wealth, and the sense is: He separates the wicked wealth that the polytheists spent from the good wealth that the Muslims spent, then He gathers those wicked wealths upon one another, casting them into Hell and punishing them with them, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿فَتُكْوى بِها جِباهُهم وجُنُوبُهم وظُهُورُهم﴾ (At-Tawbah: 35).

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The *lām* (لام) on this view is related to His saying ﴿ثُمَّ تَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ حَسْرَةً﴾, and on the first view it is related to *yuḥsharūn* (يُحْشَرُونَ). The indicator ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to those who disbelieved. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهم وهم يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ﴾, then He excepted the people of polytheism, saying: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾, that he said: Their punishment is the conquest of Makkah.

Ibn Ishaq and Abu Hatim narrated from ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ while they deny the signs of God and deny His messengers.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾: that is, whoever believes in God and worships Him, you and whoever follows you. ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾: those who leave it and establish prayer at it, that is, you and whoever believes in you.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾ that he said: Those who are wherever they are.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: The Quraysh used to oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) during the circumambulation, mocking, whistling and clapping. Then this was revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Quraysh used to circumambulate the Kaʿbah naked, whistling and clapping. So God revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. He said: *al-mukā'* is whistling; they were only likened to the whistling of birds. "*Tasdiyah*" is clapping. And God revealed about them: ﴿قُلْ مَن حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Aʿraf: 32), the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated similar to this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated similar to this from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: *al-mukā'* is whistling, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling; they mix all of that together, mixing their prayer before Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird called *al-mukkā'*, found in the land of the Hijaz, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying "*illā mukkā'an*" (إلّا مُكّاءً): he said: They used to interlace their fingers and whistle through them. "*Wa tasdiyatan*" (وتَصْدِيَةً): he said: their hindering of people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: The polytheists used to circumambulate the House keeping it on their left. This is His saying: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. So *al-mukā'* is like the blowing of a horn, and *al-tasdiyah* is their circumambulating it on the left.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His saying ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ that he said: It means the people of Badr. God punished them with killing and capture.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalā'il* all narrated through his chain: He said: al-Zuhri, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatadah and al-Husayn ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAmr told me, saying: When the Quraysh were struck on the day of Badr and their remnant returned to Makkah, and Abu Sufyan returned with his caravan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Rabiʿah, ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Safwan ibn Umayyah walked, with men from the Quraysh whose fathers and sons had been struck. They spoke to Abu Sufyan and to those among the Quraysh who had trade in that caravan, and said: O assembly of the Quraysh, Muhammad has wronged you and killed your best men. So support war against him with this wealth, so that perhaps we may take revenge from him. They did so. Concerning them, as Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned, God revealed: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ up to ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: This verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similar to this from Mujahid.

These and others narrated similar to this from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hakam ibn ʿUtaybah regarding the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who spent forty *ūqiyyah* of gold on the polytheists of the Quraysh on the day of Uhud. The *ūqiyyah* at that time was forty-two *mithqāl* of gold.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shimr ibn ʿAtiyyah regarding His saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ﴾, that he said: On the Day of Resurrection He will separate whatever good deeds were done in the world; then the entire world will be taken and cast into Hell.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ that he said: He gathers it all together.

He (glorified is He) explained that what prevents their punishment is the two matters mentioned earlier: the presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them, and the seeking of forgiveness. Then he mentioned that these disbelievers, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah, deserve God's punishment for the vile deeds they committed.

The meaning is: What is there for them that would prevent their punishment? Al-Akhfash said: The particle *an* (أنْ) is superfluous.

Al-Nahhas said: If it were as he said, it would make *yu'adhdhibahum* (يُعَذِّبَهم) nominative. The clause ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): that is, "And what prevents their punishment, while they bar people from the Sacred Mosque?" This happened in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, when they prevented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions from the House. The clause ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause referring to the subject of *yasuddūn* (يَصُدُّونَ). This is a refutation of their claim that they are the custodians of the House and that its affairs are entrusted to them. Then he said, clarifying who has that right: ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾, meaning: His protectors are only those who are among the God-fearing, who avoid polytheism and sins. ﴿ولَكِنَّ أكْثَرَهم لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (but most of them do not know this). Passing judgement on the majority as ignorant implies that a minority do know, but they are obstinate.

Regarding ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾: *al-mukā'* (المُكاءُ) means whistling, from *makā yamkū mukāan*, and from it is the verse of ʿAntarah:

*And a friend of a flirtatious woman, I left him slain, his diaphragm whistling like the cut of al-Aʿlam's jaw.*

That is, it makes a sound. From it comes *makat ist al-dābbah* (مَكَتِ اسْتُ الدّابَّةِ), when the animal's rear expels wind. It is said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird in the Hijaz called *al-mukkā'*. A poet said:

*When the mukkā' sings in a place without foliage, woe to the people of sheep and donkeys.*

*Al-tasdiyah* (التَّصْدِيَةُ) means clapping. One says *ṣadda yuṣaddī tasdiyatan* when he claps. From it is the saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Iṭnābah:

*They all remained, with an uproar for them, a whistling by the House, with clapping.*

That is, with clapping. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is striking with the hands, and *al-tasdiyah* is shouting. It is also said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling. It is also said: *al-tasdiyah* is their preventing people from the House. It is said that the original form on this view is *tasdidah*, and one of the two *dāl*s was changed into a *yā'*.

The meaning of the verse is that the polytheists used to whistle and clap at the House, which is the place of prayer and worship. They put that in place of prayer, intending thereby to distract the Muslims who were praying. It has been recited with the accusative *ṣalātahum* (صَلاتَهم) as the predicate of *kāna* (كانَ), with what follows it as its subject.

Regarding ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾: this is a shift to addressing the disbelievers, as a threat to them and to intensify terror in their hearts. What is meant is the punishment of this world, such as on the day of Badr, and the punishment of the Hereafter.

Regarding ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾: when He (glorified is He) finished describing the states of these disbelievers in bodily acts of obedience, He followed it with describing their states in financial acts of obedience.

The meaning is: the aim of these disbelievers in spending their wealth is to bar people from the path of truth by fighting the Messenger of God (ﷺ), gathering armies for that, and spending their wealth on them. This is what happened from the Quraysh disbelievers on the day of Badr, the day of Uhud, and the day of the Confederates (al-Aḥzāb), for the leaders used to spend their wealth on the army. Then God (glorified is He) informed about the unseen in a miraculous manner, saying: ﴿فَسَيُنْفِقُونَها﴾ (so they will spend it), meaning this spending will take place from them, and then the outcome of that will be that their spending becomes a regret for them. It is as if the wealth itself turns into regret, becoming remorse. Then, in the end, they will be overcome, as God promised in verses such as His saying: ﴿كَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَأغْلِبَنَّ أنا ورُسُلِي﴾ (Al-Mujadila: 21).

The meaning of *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then") in both places is either a delay in time, referring to the distance between the aforementioned spending and the emergence of the state of Islam, or a delay in rank, referring to the gap between giving up wealth and the non-attainment of the goal, which is the total opposite of it. Then He said: ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾, meaning they persisted in disbelief. This is because among those disbelievers mentioned earlier were some who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good. That is, they are driven toward it and not toward anything else.

Then He explained the reason for which He did to them what He did, saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ﴾, meaning the wicked group of disbelievers from the good group, who are the believers. ﴿ويَجْعَلَ الخَبِيثَ بَعْضَهُ عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾, meaning He makes the wicked group of disbelievers piled upon one another. ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ is an expression for gathering and joining: that is, He gathers some of them upon others and joins some of them to others, until they heap up because of their extreme crowding. One says *rakama al-shay' yarkumuhu* when he gathers it and places some of it upon other parts. The indication of ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to the wicked group, ﴿هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾, meaning those who are complete in loss. It has also been said: *al-khabīth* (الخَبِيثُ) and *al-ṭayyib* (الطَّيِّبُ) are attributes of wealth, and the sense is: He separates the wicked wealth that the polytheists spent from the good wealth that the Muslims spent, then He gathers those wicked wealths upon one another, casting them into Hell and punishing them with them, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿فَتُكْوى بِها جِباهُهم وجُنُوبُهم وظُهُورُهم﴾ (At-Tawbah: 35).

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The *lām* (لام) on this view is related to His saying ﴿ثُمَّ تَكُونُ عَلَيْهِمْ حَسْرَةً﴾, and on the first view it is related to *yuḥsharūn* (يُحْشَرُونَ). The indicator ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ refers to those who disbelieved. End of quote.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿وما كانَ اللَّهُ مُعَذِّبَهم وهم يَسْتَغْفِرُونَ﴾, then He excepted the people of polytheism, saying: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾.

Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾, that he said: Their punishment is the conquest of Makkah.

Ibn Ishaq and Abu Hatim narrated from ʿAbbad ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr: ﴿وما لَهم ألّا يُعَذِّبَهُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ while they deny the signs of God and deny His messengers.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr regarding His saying ﴿وهم يَصُدُّونَ عَنِ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ﴾: that is, whoever believes in God and worships Him, you and whoever follows you. ﴿وما كانُوا أوْلِياءَهُ إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾: those who leave it and establish prayer at it, that is, you and whoever believes in you.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid regarding His saying ﴿إنْ أوْلِياؤُهُ إلّا المُتَّقُونَ﴾ that he said: Those who are wherever they are.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: The Quraysh used to oppose the Prophet (ﷺ) during the circumambulation, mocking, whistling and clapping. Then this was revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Quraysh used to circumambulate the Kaʿbah naked, whistling and clapping. So God revealed: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. He said: *al-mukā'* is whistling; they were only likened to the whistling of birds. "*Tasdiyah*" is clapping. And God revealed about them: ﴿قُلْ مَن حَرَّمَ زِينَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ (Al-Aʿraf: 32), the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated similar to this from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated similar to this from him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he said: *al-mukā'* is whistling, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, who said: *al-mukā'* is putting their fingers into their mouths, and *al-tasdiyah* is whistling; they mix all of that together, mixing their prayer before Muhammad (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, who said: *al-mukā'* is whistling in imitation of a white bird called *al-mukkā'*, found in the land of the Hijaz, and *al-tasdiyah* is clapping.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Saʿid ibn Jubayr regarding His saying "*illā mukkā'an*" (إلّا مُكّاءً): he said: They used to interlace their fingers and whistle through them. "*Wa tasdiyatan*" (وتَصْدِيَةً): he said: their hindering of people.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from ʿIkrimah, who said: The polytheists used to circumambulate the House keeping it on their left. This is His saying: ﴿وما كانَ صَلاتُهم عِنْدَ البَيْتِ إلّا مُكاءً وتَصْدِيَةً﴾. So *al-mukā'* is like the blowing of a horn, and *al-tasdiyah* is their circumambulating it on the left.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Ḍaḥḥāk regarding His saying ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ that he said: It means the people of Badr. God punished them with killing and capture.

Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dalā'il* all narrated through his chain: He said: al-Zuhri, Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban, ʿAsim ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatadah and al-Husayn ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAmr told me, saying: When the Quraysh were struck on the day of Badr and their remnant returned to Makkah, and Abu Sufyan returned with his caravan, ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Rabiʿah, ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl and Safwan ibn Umayyah walked, with men from the Quraysh whose fathers and sons had been struck. They spoke to Abu Sufyan and to those among the Quraysh who had trade in that caravan, and said: O assembly of the Quraysh, Muhammad has wronged you and killed your best men. So support war against him with this wealth, so that perhaps we may take revenge from him. They did so. Concerning them, as Ibn ʿAbbas mentioned, God revealed: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهم لِيَصُدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ up to ﴿والَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا إلى جَهَنَّمَ يُحْشَرُونَ﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: This verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh narrated similar to this from Mujahid.

These and others narrated similar to this from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Hakam ibn ʿUtaybah regarding the verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who spent forty *ūqiyyah* of gold on the polytheists of the Quraysh on the day of Uhud. The *ūqiyyah* at that time was forty-two *mithqāl* of gold.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Shimr ibn ʿAtiyyah regarding His saying: ﴿لِيَمِيزَ اللَّهُ الخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ﴾, that he said: On the Day of Resurrection He will separate whatever good deeds were done in the world; then the entire world will be taken and cast into Hell.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd regarding His saying ﴿فَيَرْكُمَهُ جَمِيعًا﴾ that he said: He gathers it all together.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 8, verses 38–40:

Allah, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say this meaning to the disbelievers, whether he said it in this wording or in other than it.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Even if it were as al-Kisa'i said, that it is in the codex of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud (ﷺ... rather, "ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud" radiyallahu ʿanhu) as "Say to those who disbelieve: if you (tantahu, with the feminine-second-person ta at the beginning, i.e. in the second person)..." the message would not have been conveyed except with those exact words.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: That is, "Say, for their sake, this statement," which is ﴿in yantahu﴾ (if they desist). Had it meant "address them," it would have been said: "in tantahu yughfar lakum" (if you desist, you will be forgiven). This is the reading of Ibn Masʿud. A similar usage is ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ (al-Ahqaf: 11), where they addressed others about them so that they would hear it. That is: if they desist from their hostility towards the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and from fighting him, by entering into Islam, ﴿they will be forgiven what has passed﴾ for them of hostility. End of quotation. It was also said that the meaning is: if they desist from disbelief.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: What prompts this interpretation is the apodosis of the condition, ﴿they will be forgiven what has passed﴾, and forgiveness of what has passed is only for one who desists from disbelief.

In this verse there is evidence that Islam wipes out what came before it. ﴿And if they return﴾ to fighting and hostility, or to the disbelief in which they are, and the return would mean continuing. ﴿Then the precedent of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ This phrase contains a warning, a threat, and an example of those among the nations of old who were destroyed by the punishment of Allah: that is, the way of Allah has already passed concerning whoever does the like of the deeds of these people from the earlier nations, that He afflicts him with punishment; so let them expect the like of that.

﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾, that is, disbelief. The explanation of this has already been given in full in al-Baqarah. ﴿And if they desist﴾ from what was mentioned, ﴿then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾, nothing of their desisting is hidden from Him. ﴿And if they turn away﴾ from what they were commanded regarding desisting, ﴿then know﴾, O believers, ﴿that Allah is your Protector﴾, that is, your Helper against them. ﴿An excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾ Whoever takes Him as ally succeeds, and whoever is helped by Him prevails.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿the precedent of the former peoples has already passed﴾, that he said: "It refers to Quraysh and others on the Day of Badr, and to the nations before that."

Ahmad and Muslim transmitted from ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said: "When Allah placed Islam in my heart, I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Extend your hand so that I may pledge allegiance to you.' He extended his right hand, but I withdrew my hand. He said: 'What is the matter with you?' I said: 'I wish to make a condition.' He said: 'What condition?' I said: 'That you forgive me.' He said: 'Do you not know that Islam wipes out what was before it, that Hijrah wipes out what was before it, and that Hajj wipes out what was before it?'"

It is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Ibn Masʿud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Islam wipes out what was before it, and repentance wipes out what was before it." Many of the early scholars explained His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿then the precedent of the former peoples has already passed﴾ as referring to what passed among the earlier nations of punishment upon those who fought the prophets and persisted in disbelief.

Al-Suddi and Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: the verse is meant of the Day of Badr.

The majority of the early scholars interpreted the fitnah mentioned here as disbelief.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: It reached me, from al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr and others of our scholars, concerning ﴿until there is no fitnah﴾: until no Muslim is tempted away from his religion.
